📌 Transaction Nonces: Why One Stuck Tx Can Block the Next Ones

Main Points
⏺ Wallet transactions are processed in a specific order
⏺ If one transaction gets stuck, later ones may wait behind it
⏺ This post explains why ordering matters and how wallet “traffic jams” happen

1️⃣ What It Is — the network tracks which transaction from an address should come next.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — ordering prevents replay issues and helps the chain process actions correctly.
3️⃣ The Problem — a low-fee transaction can get stuck, blocking later transactions from the same wallet.
4️⃣ User Options — speed it up, replace it, or cancel it with a new transaction using the same nonce.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — don’t fire multiple transactions blindly, and always check fees before signing.

Final Thoughts

In blockchains, the transaction itself matters — but so does its place in line. One weak step can freeze the whole flow after it.

📌 Tether Q2 profit hits $1.5B as USDT supply grows 

⚠️ Tether generated approximately $1.5 billion in net operating profit during the second quarter of 2026 as returns from US Treasury holdings and repo operations supported its earnings. The figures appeared in Tether’s latest reserve attestation, prepared by accounting firm BDO and released Friday. US government-backed securities continued to account for the largest portion of the company’s reserve portfolio. 

🌐 Interest earned from that portfolio, along with returns from repo operations, provided the main source of Tether’s second-quarter profit. The company’s exposure to short-term US debt has made its earnings sensitive to Federal Reserve policy and changes in Treasury yields. Tether also reported that the circulating supply of USDT reached approximately $184.6 billion by the end of June. Based on the company’s figures, the token controlled more than 60% of the global stablecoin market.

🔗 Tether adjusted the composition of its reserves during the quarter by reducing secured lending and increasing its holdings of physical gold. Outstanding secured loans fell by about $2.4 billion. Tether did not provide a full breakdown of the borrowers or collateral involved in the lending reduction in the information accompanying the results.

Washington spent decades turning the dollar into a global chokehold. Now it's discovering that chokeholds make people want out — and calling that discovery a national security threat.

Vladimir Putin's pitch for years has been simple: "The dollar is being used as a weapon. We really see that this is so. 

I think that this is a big mistake by those who do this" (Binance/BRICS Summit Kazan). Fair point on paper — coming from a man who's been building his SWIFT exit and stacking gold reserves since 2014, well before this invasion, precisely because he always knew the dollar system could be turned off for him the moment it mattered. 

Trump's response to the "threat" of countries wanting financial sovereignty has been to threaten... financial punishment. 

"You leave the dollar, you're not doing business with the United States because we're going to put 100 percent tariff on your goods," he warned, later escalating to comparing the dollar's dominance to winning "a major world war" (Peterson Institute, YouTube/Fox). 

Nothing defends the free market quite like threatening tariffs on anyone who tries to leave it.

Meanwhile the bloc claiming to build "financial sovereignty" can't agree on what it's actually building. 

Putin insists de-dollarization is "irreversible" and that Russia now settles roughly 65% of its exports in rubles. 

His own spokesman Dmitry Peskov, on the same week Trump threatened tariffs, told reporters BRICS "is not talking about creating a common currency, nor has it ever done so" — and suggested US experts "explain the BRICS agenda in more detail to Mr. Trump". 

India's foreign ministry went further, flatly denying any de-dollarization policy at all — from a government whose central bank is simultaneously running live cross-border settlement tests with China, Egypt, and the UAE that route zero dollars through zero clearinghouses.

Russia says the revolution is unstoppable, its own spokesman says there's no revolution, India says it isn't participating in the revolution while quietly building the revolution's plumbing, and the country most terrified of the revolution is the one guaranteeing it happens faster by threatening everyone with the exact weapon they're trying to escape.

Nobody in this story is building sovereignty. Everybody's just building a backup generator for the day the main power gets cut — and hoping nobody asks who flipped the switch in the first place.

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.
